title: Cotton Personal-Care Product Manufacturing
one_liner: A small, mature U.S. manufacturing niche making cotton swabs, balls, pads, rounds, gauze and related first-aid or beauty-aid cotton products.
overview: This industry manufactures cotton-based personal-care and medical-use consumables, including cotton swabs, cotton balls, cosmetic rounds and squares, absorbent cotton, gauze, dressings and related first-aid cotton items. The domestic manufacturing base is small because products are standardized, low-margin and easy to source globally. Demand is recurring and relatively inelastic in medical and household uses, while beauty and skincare routines create higher-value opportunities for organic cotton, quilted pads, premium rounds and specialized swabs. Current 2025-2026 conditions are better on demand than on domestic volume: U.S. personal-care spending and beauty retail sales are rising, but imports, retailer private labels and offshore cost advantages continue to cap U.S. manufacturing growth.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: about $280 million in U.S. manufacturer revenue, current dollars; this is derived from the IBISWorld baseline forecast of about $224.7 million for 2024 in 2019 dollars and adjusted to 2025 dollars.
key_stats.growth: 2025: roughly flat real growth, about 0% real volume growth; nominal revenue supported mainly by price inflation rather than unit expansion.
key_stats.domestic_demand: 2019: $294 million in 2019 dollars in the baseline file; demand exceeded domestic shipments because imports supplied a large share of consumption.
key_stats.imports: 2019: $186 million in 2019 dollars in the baseline file, equal to about 63.1% of domestic demand.
key_stats.exports: 2019: $117 million in 2019 dollars in the baseline file, equal to about 51.8% of industry revenue.
key_stats.input_price: 2026/27: USDA projected world cotton prices at about 90 cents per pound, up from about 80 cents per pound in each of the prior two seasons.
key_stats.consumer_demand_proxy: 2025: BEA personal consumption expenditures for personal-care products reached $213.592 billion, up from $203.421 billion in 2024.
key_stats.beauty_channel_proxy: 2025: Circana reported U.S. prestige beauty retail dollar sales of $36.0 billion, up 4%, and mass beauty sales of $72.7 billion, up 5%.
key_stats.healthcare_demand_proxy: 2024: CMS reported U.S. national health expenditures of $5.3 trillion, up 7.2%; CMS projected 2025-2034 national health expenditure growth averaging 5.4% per year.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: about $224.9 million in 2019 dollars, or about $259 million in current dollars, estimated from the baseline file's 2019 revenue of $225.6 million and 2019-2024 forecast decline of about 0.1% CAGR.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: approximately flat to -0.1% real growth on the baseline forecast path.
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 2019 baseline: 4.7% EBIT margin, down from 6.6% in 2014 because cotton costs and imports pressured profitability.
baseline_2022.trade_position: 2019 baseline: imports of $186 million exceeded exports of $117 million, producing a structural trade deficit.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue by converting raw or processed cotton into high-volume disposable products sold to retailers, private-label programs, distributors, hospitals, clinics, beauty brands and first-aid brands. Retail-facing manufacturers make money through branded swabs, pads and cotton balls; private-label manufacturers make money through large-volume contracts for drug, grocery, club, dollar and mass-merchandise chains; medical suppliers earn through gauze, dressings and sterile cotton products sold through healthcare procurement channels.

cost_structure.materials: 2019 baseline and 2026 update: cotton fiber, paper or plastic sticks, packaging film, cartons, adhesives, sterilization inputs and freight are the key variable costs; cotton price volatility remains the main commodity risk.
cost_structure.labor: 2019 baseline: wages were about $40 million, or roughly 17.7% of 2019 revenue; automation continues to reduce labor intensity in swab, pad and ball lines.
cost_structure.profit: 2019 baseline: EBIT margin was 4.7%; 2025-2026 margins remain constrained by retailer bargaining power, import competition, freight, packaging and cotton costs.
cost_structure.sales_and_distribution: 2025-2026: slotting, retailer programs, ecommerce fulfillment, private-label service requirements and medical-distribution compliance absorb a meaningful share of gross margin.
cost_structure.capital: 2025-2026: automated converting, carding, quilting, packaging, sterilization and quality-control equipment are needed to compete on unit cost and consistency.

major_players: Evermark LLC / Yellow Wood Partners - Q-tips brand owner after the 2024 Elida Beauty acquisition and 2026 Evermark merger
U.S. Cotton LLC - major U.S. health and beauty cotton products and private-label manufacturer
Kenvue Inc. - BAND-AID and wound-care products including gauze and first-aid items
Medline Industries - medical gauze, dressings and healthcare consumables supplier
Retail private labels - Walmart, Target, Walgreens, CVS, dollar stores and grocery chains source large volumes of cotton swabs, balls and pads
current_dynamics: Demand is stable to modestly positive in 2025-2026 because beauty, skincare, household hygiene and healthcare consumption keep recurring purchases high. The strongest consumer tailwind is beauty: U.S. mass beauty grew 5% in 2025 and prestige beauty grew 4%, supporting cotton rounds, pads and precision swabs used for skincare, makeup and nail care. Healthcare demand is also supportive, with 2024 national health spending up 7.2% and 2025-2034 spending projected to grow 5.4% annually. The main constraint is domestic manufacturing share: low-cost imported swabs, pads and cotton balls, especially from Asia and nearshore suppliers, limit pricing power. 2025 China tariff and de minimis changes may help domestic or nearshore suppliers at the margin, but retailer buyers still pressure manufacturers to hold prices down.
whats_growing: Organic cotton swabs and rounds, quilted and lint-resistant cosmetic pads, premium beauty rounds, paper-stick swabs replacing plastic-stick formats, private-label programs, ecommerce replenishment packs, first-aid gauze and wound-care cotton products tied to aging and outpatient-care demand, and retailer-exclusive or seasonal branded SKUs are growing in 2025-2026.
whats_shrinking: Commodity-grade branded cotton balls and basic swabs are losing share to private labels and value packs. U.S. unit manufacturing of highly standardized products is shrinking or staying flat where imports can meet retailer specs at lower cost. Plastic-stick swabs face environmental and retailer preference pressure, and low-differentiation small manufacturers continue to struggle against scale players and store brands.
recent_developments: 2024-06: Yellow Wood Partners completed its acquisition of Unilever's Elida Beauty portfolio, including Q-tips, moving a major cotton-swab brand out of Unilever.

2025-02: U.S. Customs and Border Protection issued guidance applying an additional 10% duty to China and Hong Kong imports and ending de minimis treatment for covered shipments, raising landed-cost uncertainty for low-value personal-care imports.
2025-12: USDA's Cotton and Wool Yearbook data update showed cotton prices and textile trade data remained central to downstream cotton-product cost planning.

2026-01: Suave Brands and Elida Beauty merged to form Evermark LLC, a personal-care platform including Q-tips, ChapStick, Ponds, St. Ives, Suave and other brands with about $1.9 billion in annual retail sales.
2026-02: Circana reported 2025 U.S. mass beauty sales of $72.7 billion, up 5%, and prestige beauty sales of $36.0 billion, up 4%, supporting demand for beauty cotton pads, rounds and swabs.
2026-06: USDA projected 2026/27 world cotton prices near 90 cents per pound, up from about 80 cents per pound in the prior two seasons, signaling higher input-cost risk for cotton converters.
outlook: The 2026-2030 outlook is for low real growth and modest nominal gains. Domestic demand should be steady because cotton pads, swabs, balls and gauze are low-ticket replenishment items used in beauty, first aid and medical care. Growth will come from premiumization, organic cotton, plastic-free formats, private-label contracts and medical/wound-care channels rather than from basic commodity volume. The domestic manufacturing base will remain under pressure from imports and retailer margin demands, but tariff uncertainty, de minimis restrictions and buyer interest in supply-chain resilience could preserve some U.S. capacity. Profitability will depend on cotton prices, packaging costs, automation, retailer mix and the ability to sell differentiated products rather than purely commodity packs.
themes: Private label and retailer bargaining power
one_sentence: In 2025-2026, U.S. cotton personal-care product manufacturing remains a flat-volume, price-sensitive industry supported by resilient beauty, household hygiene and medical demand but pressured by imports, private label competition, and cotton/input cost volatility.

title: Cough & Cold Medicine Manufacturing OTC
one_liner: U.S. OTC cough and cold medicine manufacturers are a mature, seasonal consumer-health industry now balancing self-care demand, retailer private labels and phenylephrine reformulation risk.
overview: This industry manufactures nonprescription cough, cold and upper-respiratory symptom products, including tablets, capsules, packets, liquid powders, cough syrups, nasal products and throat drops. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline put U.S. manufacturing revenue at $11.488 billion, with 2022 growth of 3.6% and projected 2022-2027 annualized growth of 2.14%. Using that baseline trend and current 2025 demand indicators, 2025 manufacturer revenue is estimated at about $12.2 billion. Retail-side evidence points to a mixed but improving demand environment: U.S. upper-respiratory OTC unit volume was 1.223 billion units in 2025, up 4.6% from 1.169 billion units in 2024 but still below the 1.317 billion-unit 2022 spike. The sector remains mature and brand-led, but growth is increasingly tied to multi-symptom formats, e-commerce access, private-label competition and manufacturers' ability to reformulate or reposition decongestant products if FDA finalizes its proposed removal of oral phenylephrine from the OTC monograph for nasal congestion.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated U.S. manufacturer revenue of $12.2 billion, based on the 2022 IBISWorld revenue baseline of $11.488 billion and the 2022-2027 projected CAGR of 2.14%.
key_stats.growth: 2025 U.S. upper-respiratory OTC retail unit volume rose 4.6% to 1.223 billion units from 1.169 billion units in 2024; 2025 U.S. cold and cough remedies retail revenue was projected at $8.61 billion by Statista Market Insights.
key_stats.profitability: 2022 IBISWorld profit margin was 9.7%, equal to $1.114 billion of profit on $11.488 billion of revenue.
key_stats.trade: 2022 IBISWorld imports were $8.025 billion and exports were $3.551 billion, showing high import penetration and meaningful global trade exposure.
key_stats.volume_context: 2025 U.S. upper-respiratory OTC volume of 1.223 billion units remained 7.1% below the 2022 level of 1.317 billion units.

baseline_2022.growth: 2022 revenue growth was 3.6%, with 2017-2022 annualized growth of 2.4% and a 2022-2027 projected CAGR of 2.14%.
baseline_2022.profit: 2022 profit was $1.114 billion and profit margin was 9.7%.
baseline_2022.employment: 2022 employment was 11,622 workers across 127 establishments and 101 enterprises.
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022 product mix was tablets and packets 56.2%, liquid powders 20.1%, nasal products 8.8%, throat drops 7.6% and cough syrup 7.3%.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue by producing branded and private-label OTC products sold through pharmacies, drug stores, mass retailers, grocery, club, dollar, convenience, military and online channels. The largest revenue pools are multi-symptom tablets, capsules and packets, followed by liquid powders, nasal products, throat drops and cough syrups. Brand owners monetize trusted names, pharmacist and physician recommendations, seasonal promotion, shelf placement and line extensions, while contract manufacturers and private-label suppliers compete on scale, formulation compliance and cost.
cost_structure: The 2022 baseline showed a capital- and compliance-heavy model with profit at 9.7% of revenue and wages at $1.421 billion. Major costs include active pharmaceutical ingredients such as acetaminophen, dextromethorphan, guaifenesin, antihistamines and decongestants; excipients, flavors and sweeteners; bottles, blister packs, cartons and packets; FDA-compliant manufacturing and testing; quality systems; logistics; retailer allowances; advertising; R&D; user fees; and reformulation costs. 2026 FDA OMUFA facility fees were $19,188 for monograph drug facilities and $12,792 for contract manufacturing organizations, down from 2025 fees of $37,556 and $25,037, respectively.
major_players: Kenvue: Tylenol, Benadryl, Zarbee's, Zyrtec and related self-care brands; 2025 global net sales were $15.1 billion, with Self Care affected by lower seasonal incidence.
Haleon: Theraflu, Robitussin, Flonase and Otrivin; 2025 Respiratory Health revenue was £1.873 billion, down 11.7% reported and down 1.9% organically.
Procter & Gamble: Vicks within Personal Health Care; fiscal 2025 company net sales were $84.3 billion and Health Care was 14% of sales.
Reckitt: Mucinex, Delsym and Strepsils respiratory brands; 2025 company like-for-like net revenue growth was 5.0%.
Prestige Consumer Healthcare: Chloraseptic, Little Remedies, Luden's and other OTC brands; fiscal 2025 portfolio served North America, Australia and other international markets.
Retail private labels: CVS, Walgreens, Walmart, Target, Costco and grocery/private-label programs pressure branded pricing and capture value-oriented demand.
current_dynamics: The industry is being pulled in two directions in 2025-2026. Consumer self-care is structurally strong, with 46% of U.S. adults reporting OTC medication use in a 2026 seven-day survey, and 2025 upper-respiratory unit volume recovered from 2024. At the same time, demand is highly seasonal: Kenvue and Haleon both cited weak 2025 cold and flu incidence in key markets, especially late in the year, and retailer inventory reductions reduced shipments. FDA's 2024 proposed order on oral phenylephrine remains the central regulatory overhang in 2026 because it could force manufacturers to reformulate or discontinue many oral decongestant SKUs if finalized. Private labels and imports continue to restrain pricing power, while e-commerce and same-day pharmacy fulfillment expand consumer access.
whats_growing: Multi-symptom combination products, adult tablets/capsules, liquid and packet formats, e-commerce fulfillment, private-label OTC lines, value packs, pharmacist-led self-care recommendations and reformulated congestion products using alternatives to oral phenylephrine are growing. 2025 U.S. upper-respiratory OTC volume increased to 1.223 billion units from 1.169 billion units in 2024, and 2025 cough/cold/allergy value sales increased after a weak 2024 season according to Euromonitor's 2025 U.S. category summary.
whats_shrinking: Pandemic-era stockpiling, 2022 peak unit volume, oral phenylephrine-dependent decongestant positioning, weaker cough-heavy products in mild seasons, and branded price premiums are under pressure. U.S. upper-respiratory OTC volume in 2025 was still below the 2022 high of 1.317 billion units. Haleon's 2025 Respiratory Health revenue fell to £1.873 billion from £2.122 billion in 2024, and Robitussin declined double digits in 2025 Q4 amid lower cough incidence.
recent_developments: 2024-11-07: FDA proposed removing oral phenylephrine from the OTC monograph for nasal congestion because the agency found it ineffective for that use.
2025-09-22: Euromonitor reported 2025 U.S. cough, cold and allergy remedies value sales increased after a weak 2024 cough and cold season and a late-January to early-February 2025 case spike.
2025-12-31: Haleon reported 2025 Respiratory Health revenue of £1.873 billion, down 11.7% reported and down 1.9% organically, with weak cold and flu incidence weighing on North America.
2026-02-18: CHPA highlighted a 2026 JAMA Network Open study finding 46% of U.S. adults used an OTC medication in the prior seven days.
2026-03-18: FDA announced FY 2026 OMUFA facility fees of $19,188 for monograph drug facilities and $12,792 for contract manufacturing organizations.
2026-05-26: CHPA/Statista reported 2025 U.S. upper-respiratory OTC volume of 1.223 billion units, up from 1.169 billion units in 2024.
outlook: Revenue should grow modestly through 2026-2027 from the $12.2 billion estimated 2025 manufacturer base, but not at pandemic-era rates. The 2022 IBISWorld forecast implied 2027 revenue of about $12.8 billion, and current data support a mature, low- to mid-single-digit path rather than a step change. Upside comes from recurring cold/flu seasons, aging consumers, broader self-care habits, online access and premium multi-symptom innovation. Downside comes from mild respiratory seasons, retailer inventory resets, import competition, private-label substitution and potential reformulation costs if FDA finalizes the oral phenylephrine order.
themes: Seasonality and respiratory incidence drive shipment volatility
FDA monograph reform and phenylephrine risk
Private-label competition and retailer bargaining power
Self-care adoption and avoided physician visits
one_sentence: In 2025, the industry benefited from a rebound in upper-respiratory OTC unit volume after a weak 2024 season, but manufacturer growth remained uneven because cold and flu incidence, retailer inventory discipline, imports and FDA scrutiny of oral phenylephrine all shaped demand.

title: Cruise & Travel Agency Franchises
one_liner: Home-based and storefront travel franchises sell cruises, vacation packages and complex leisure trips, with cruise demand and advisor-led planning driving the post-pandemic recovery.
overview: The industry includes franchised travel agencies and cruise-focused advisor networks that arrange cruises, packaged tours, resorts, accommodation, transport and related services for leisure and some business travelers. The 2021 IBISWorld baseline described a sharp pandemic contraction to $1.5 billion of revenue in 2021, followed by a recovery forecast as cruise ships returned and consumers resumed discretionary travel. By 2025, public franchise listings citing IBISWorld put the US cruise and travel agency franchise market at about $3.0 billion and over 8,000 businesses, broadly consistent with the baseline recovery path toward about $3.2 billion by 2026. The franchise model is heavily home-based, low-inventory and advisor-led, but it competes with online travel agencies and supplier-direct booking sites; its strongest niche is complex, high-value travel where consumers value human advice, itinerary design, disruption support and cruise-specific expertise.

key_stats.market_size: 2025: about $3.0 billion in US cruise and travel agency franchise revenue
key_stats.growth: 2025: about 5.2% year-over-year growth in broader US travel arrangement and reservation services revenue, based on Census/FRED quarterly revenue rising from $88.5 billion in 2024 to $93.1 billion in 2025
key_stats.businesses: 2025: over 8,000 US cruise and travel agency franchise businesses cited by Franchise Direct from IBISWorld research
key_stats.broader_agency_sales: 2025: ARC-accredited US travel agency air ticket sales reached $100.4 billion, up 1% from 2024
key_stats.cruise_volume: 2025: 37.2 million global cruise passengers sailed, a historic high reported by CLIA in 2026
key_stats.advisor_channel: 2025: 67% of surveyed US travel advisors were home-based independent contractors or agencies, according to Travel Weekly/Phocuswright
key_stats.outbound_travel: 2024: US resident outbound travelers totaled a record 107.7 million, up 9.2% from 2023

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: about $1.7 billion, estimated from the 2021 IBISWorld baseline revenue of $1.5 billion and its 2021-2026 recovery trajectory
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: about 16.6% estimated recovery growth from the 2021 baseline trajectory
baseline_2022.businesses: 2022: 38 enterprises in the US cruise and travel agency franchise industry, up from 30 in 2021, according to Statista citing IBISWorld
baseline_2022.context: 2022 was an early recovery year after the 2020 no-sail period and the 2021 partial restart of US cruising.

how_it_makes_money: Franchisees earn supplier commissions, overrides and sometimes service or planning fees from cruise lines, tour operators, resorts, hotels, car rental firms, travel insurers and package suppliers. Franchisors earn initial franchise fees, royalties, technology or marketing fees, preferred-supplier overrides and training or support fees. Cruise and tour bookings are especially important because ticket values are high and customers are more likely to use advisors for multi-leg, group, luxury, expedition, accessible or international trips.
cost_structure: The model has low inventory and modest physical-plant needs, especially for home-based agencies. Major costs are owner labor and advisor commissions, franchise royalties and marketing fees, reservation and CRM technology, lead generation, training, insurance, professional memberships, payment processing, and limited rent for storefront brands. Margins are pressured by supplier commission changes, customer-acquisition costs, refund and rebooking workload, and competition from online travel agencies, but home-based operations keep fixed costs lower than traditional storefront agencies.
major_players: Cruise Planners
Dream Vacations / CruiseOne, part of World Travel Holdings
Expedia Cruises
Travel Leaders Network / Internova Travel Group
Avoya Travel
Cruises Inc. legacy network within World Travel Holdings
current_dynamics: Demand is strong but more normalized than the immediate post-pandemic rebound. Cruise is the key demand engine: CLIA reported 37.2 million global passengers in 2025, nearly 90% repeat intent, and 325 CLIA-member ocean-going ships expected in 2026. Agency-channel proof points are also solid, with 2025 ARC-accredited US agency air ticket sales at $100.4 billion and 292.9 million passenger trips. The operating model is shifting toward home-based advisors and independent contractors: the 2025 Travel Weekly/Phocuswright survey found 67% of respondents were home-based independents, while large networks are adding members to provide technology, supplier leverage, leads and education. At the same time, 2026 data show some softness in US outbound air departures in individual months, so revenue growth is more dependent on higher-value cruise, luxury, group and packaged travel than on simple air-ticket volume.
whats_growing: Luxury, premium, expedition, river and multigenerational cruises; complex international itineraries; group travel; destination weddings; all-inclusive resorts; advisor service fees; home-based franchise ownership; AI-assisted marketing, CRM and itinerary planning; and consortia/host-network services that give small agencies supplier access and technology scale.
whats_shrinking: Simple point-to-point airline ticketing, unmanaged hotel-only bookings, low-value domestic weekend trips, walk-in storefront dependence, paper-heavy back-office workflows, and commission-only economics for advisors who cannot add planning value or charge service fees.
recent_developments: 2025-02: Expedia Cruises said it surpassed 260 locations after 2024 growth and planned 15 additional awards in 2025.
2025-05: CLIA projected 37.7 million global cruise passengers for 2025 and reported 34.6 million passengers in 2024.
2025-09: NTTO reported 8.55 million US citizen international departures for September 2025, up 0.5% from September 2024.
2026-01: ARC reported US travel agency air ticket sales reached $100.4 billion in 2025, up 1% from 2024.
2026-01: Travel Leaders Network said it added more than 300 member agencies in 2025, including 264 US affiliates.
2026-04: CLIA reported actual 2025 global cruise passenger volume of 37.2 million and $75 billion of 2024 US cruise economic impact.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is positive but slower than the 2021-2024 rebound phase. Cruise capacity, high repeat intent, new ships, private-destination investment and younger/new-to-cruise customers support continued demand for cruise-specialist franchises. The industry should keep gaining from consumers outsourcing complex trips, but growth is likely to moderate as outbound air demand normalizes, prices remain high and online self-booking continues to capture simpler transactions. Franchisors with strong supplier relationships, advisor training, AI-enabled marketing, lead routing and service-fee discipline should outperform small operators that rely on undifferentiated commission bookings.
themes: Travel disruption support as value proposition
one_sentence: Cruise & Travel Agency Franchises in the US are small, franchised travel-advisor businesses that earn commissions and fees from cruises, tours, resorts, air and packaged travel, with 2025 demand supported by record cruise volume, resilient outbound travel and the continued shift toward home-based advisors.

title: DNA & DNA Forensic Laboratories
one_liner: DNA labs are still growing, but the mix is shifting from consumer curiosity tests toward forensic capacity, relationship testing, clinical genomics and automated high-throughput lab work.
overview: This industry provides DNA paternity and relationship testing, forensic DNA analysis, ancestry and family relationship testing, veterinary DNA testing and related human-genetics laboratory services; it excludes state-owned, law-enforcement-owned and public university laboratories. The 2020 IBISWorld baseline placed 2020 revenue at $3.3 billion and forecast 2025 revenue of $4.2 billion, with 2020 revenue split across legal forensic services at 42.9%, discretionary paternity testing at 37.5%, ancestry/family relationship testing at 15.5% and veterinary DNA testing at 4.1%. In 2025-2026, the strongest demand signals are law-enforcement DNA processing, CODIS participation, rapid DNA workflows, clinical/specialty genetic testing and health-system lab outsourcing; the weakest signal is mass-market direct-to-consumer ancestry testing after 23andMe's 2025 bankruptcy sale.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated US industry revenue: $4.2 billion, based on the baseline 2020 IBISWorld forecast for DNA & DNA Forensic Laboratories.
key_stats.growth: 2020-2025 estimated revenue CAGR: 5.0%, based on the baseline IBISWorld forecast.
key_stats.forensic_database_scale: November 2025 FBI NDIS contained 19,272,496 offender profiles, 6,142,751 arrestee profiles and 1,449,731 forensic profiles.
key_stats.codis_output: November 2025 FBI CODIS had produced more than 781,492 hits and assisted more than 758,449 investigations.
key_stats.birth_demand_indicator: 2025 provisional US births were 3,606,400, down 1% from 2024; 2024 births to unmarried women were 39.5% of all births.
key_stats.lab_reimbursement: 2026 CMS CLFS rules had no phase-in reduction in 2026; 2027-2029 reductions are capped at 15% per test per year.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 estimated US industry revenue: $3.6 billion, derived from the baseline 2020 revenue of $3.296 billion and the baseline 2020-2025 forecast CAGR of 5.0%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 estimated annual growth: 5.0%, using the baseline IBISWorld 2020-2025 forecast CAGR.
baseline_2022.context: The 2020 baseline expected growth from falling DNA test costs, higher lab throughput, paternity testing accessibility, outsourced forensic casework and ancestry/family relationship testing.

how_it_makes_money: Labs earn revenue by charging consumers, attorneys, courts, hospitals, clinics, law-enforcement agencies, government buyers, veterinarians and research/health partners for DNA sample collection, accessioning, extraction, amplification, sequencing or STR profiling, interpretation, chain-of-custody documentation, expert reporting and secure data delivery. Forensic and legal paternity work often earns higher fees because accreditation, review, documentation and court-admissible handling are required; discretionary paternity and ancestry tests compete more heavily on price and turnaround time.
cost_structure: Major 2025-2026 costs are skilled laboratory labor, genetic analysts, quality managers, reagents, collection kits, sequencing/STR instruments, lab automation, software, accreditation, CLIA/CAP/ISO compliance, cybersecurity, insurance, logistics and sample storage. The baseline model showed high profitability versus many laboratory services because automation and throughput reduce unit costs, but margins remain exposed to wage inflation, reagent prices, instrument depreciation, privacy/security costs and Medicare/private-payer reimbursement pressure under CLFS/PAMA.
major_players: Labcorp
Quest Diagnostics
DNA Diagnostics Center
Bode Technology
Eurofins Scientific
23andMe Research Institute / TTAM Research Institute
AncestryDNA
Thermo Fisher Scientific, QIAGEN, Promega and Illumina as key forensic DNA suppliers rather than pure-play labs
current_dynamics: Forensic demand is supported by CODIS expansion, cold-case work, sexual-assault-kit processing, Rapid DNA adoption and DOJ/BJA backlog-reduction funding. Consumer paternity and legal relationship testing remain steadier than ancestry because legal, child-support, immigration and custody needs are less discretionary. Clinical and specialty genetics are benefiting from health-system outsourcing and large commercial labs' advanced diagnostics strategies. Direct-to-consumer ancestry remains pressured after 23andMe's 2025 bankruptcy and privacy concerns, although its assets continued under TTAM/23andMe Research Institute.
whats_growing: 2025 forensic DNA outsourcing and backlog-reduction work tied to CODIS and BJA CEBR funding.
2025-2026 Rapid DNA workflows, including FBI forensic casework QAS effective July 1, 2025.
2025-2026 specialty genetic and molecular testing within large commercial lab networks.
2025-2026 health-system and regional-lab outsourcing by Labcorp and Quest Diagnostics.
2025-2026 privacy-aware research services using consented genetic datasets.
whats_shrinking: 2025-2026 mass-market direct-to-consumer ancestry testing demand after 23andMe's bankruptcy sale and prior privacy concerns.
2025-2026 price per routine DNA test as automation, competition and sequencing throughput improve.
2025-2026 birth-linked paternity testing volume potential because provisional US births declined 1% in 2025 to 3,606,400.
2027 risk: Medicare CLFS payment reductions resume with a 15% annual cap after no reduction in 2026.
recent_developments: 2025-07-01: FBI national QAS and procedures for Rapid DNA forensic casework became effective for CODIS-eligible forensic samples.
2025-07-14: TTAM Research Institute completed the acquisition of 23andMe's Personal Genome Service and Research Services assets for a reported $305.0 million bankruptcy sale price.
2025-09-11: BJA posted FY25 DNA Capacity Enhancement for Backlog Reduction funding opportunities to increase DNA sample processing and prevent forensic DNA backlogs.
2025-11: FBI reported NDIS totals of 19.27 million offender profiles, 6.14 million arrestee profiles and 1.45 million forensic profiles.
2026-02-03: CMS said CAA 2026 delayed CLFS private-payor-rate reductions, with no 2026 phase-in reduction and a 15% annual reduction cap for 2027-2029.
2026-07-23: Quest Diagnostics raised 2026 revenue guidance to $11.95 billion-$12.05 billion after Q2 2026 revenue rose 10.2% year over year.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is positive but uneven. Industry revenue should keep expanding from forensic demand, CODIS database activity, Rapid DNA adoption, lab outsourcing, and specialty genetic testing, while consumer ancestry remains a weaker growth pocket. Price competition will keep routine paternity and consumer tests from expanding as fast as volumes, and 2027 CLFS reimbursement resets may pressure labs with Medicare exposure. Larger players are likely to keep consolidating regional lab capacity and investing in automation, privacy controls and high-throughput platforms.
one_sentence: The US DNA & DNA Forensic Laboratories industry generated an estimated $4.2 billion in 2025 revenue, up at an estimated 5.0% 2020-2025 CAGR from the 2020 IBISWorld baseline, with forensic backlogs, CODIS expansion, paternity demand and specialty genetic testing offsetting softer direct-to-consumer ancestry demand.

title: DVD, Game & Video Rental in the US
one_liner: A once-mainstream rental channel has become a residual niche after streaming absorbed mass demand and the last national disc-rental networks shut down.
overview: This industry rents prerecorded DVDs, Blu-ray discs, videos and physical video games for home use, including vending-machine rental, and excludes internet-streamed rentals. Its economics have been structurally impaired by subscription streaming, premium VOD, digital game stores and declining retail support for physical media. Census/FRED revenue for video tape and disc rental was $662 million in 2022, down 17.7% from 2021. Using BLS/FRED 2025 employment-index data as a current proxy, the 2025 market is estimated at about $370 million, with a sharp 2025 decline following the 2024 Redbox liquidation.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated revenue: $370 million, modeled from 2022 Census/FRED revenue of $662 million scaled by the BLS/FRED NAICS 532282 employment index falling from 33.010 in 2022 to 18.447 in 2025.
key_stats.growth: 2025 estimated revenue proxy: -29.6% versus 2024, matching the BLS/FRED NAICS 532282 employment-index decline from 26.214 in 2024 to 18.447 in 2025.
key_stats.employment_signal: 2025 BLS/FRED employment index for NAICS 532282: 18.447, down from 26.214 in 2024 and 33.010 in 2022, index 2017=100.
key_stats.adjacent_physical_media: 2025 US physical home-entertainment sell-through spending: $870 million, down 9.3% from 2024, according to DEG; this excludes rentals.
key_stats.streaming_substitute: 2025 US subscription streaming spending: $57.5 billion, up 19.8% from 2024 and more than 92% of US home-entertainment consumer spending, according to DEG.
key_stats.video_game_substitute: 2025 US consumer spending on video games: $60.8 billion, up from $59.3 billion in 2024, according to ESA/Circana/Sensor Tower; subscription services grew 20% in 2025.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 Census/FRED total revenue for video tape and disc rental employer firms: $662 million.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 revenue declined 17.7% from 2021 Census/FRED revenue of $804 million.
baseline_2022.sectoral_output: 2022 BLS/FRED sectoral output for NAICS 532282: $698.223 million.
baseline_2022.industry_condition: IBISWorld baseline file projected ongoing decline, with 2021 revenue of $1.041 billion and a 2021-2026 forecast CAGR of about -14.7% to $470.9 million in 2026.

how_it_makes_money: Operators make money from one-off disc and game rentals, subscription rental plans, late or replacement fees, used-disc sales, niche catalog memberships, event rentals and small add-on sales such as collectibles or movie/game merchandise. The 2021 baseline mix was 64.4% non-subscription rental, 33.1% subscription rental and 2.5% other revenue, but the 2023 Netflix DVD exit and 2024 Redbox liquidation shifted the remaining market toward local, specialty and long-tail catalog rentals.
cost_structure: The largest remaining cost pressures are title acquisition and licensing, kiosk or store rent, labor for customer service and inventory handling, distribution/postage where mail rental remains, kiosk maintenance, payment processing, inventory shrinkage and depreciation on physical media and vending assets. The baseline 2021 profit margin was only 2.7%, reflecting heavy price pressure from streaming and digital rentals; 2025 economics are weaker for scale operators because national kiosk density and studio-disc supply have collapsed.
major_players: No current national-scale US physical disc rental chain remains after Redbox shut down in 2024.
Redbox Automated Retail LLC: legacy national kiosk leader; parent Chicken Soup for the Soul Entertainment converted to Chapter 7 liquidation in July 2024.
Netflix DVD / DVD.com: legacy subscription-by-mail leader; final discs shipped September 29, 2023.
Independent specialty video stores and local rental collections, including cinephile, archive, horror, foreign-film and out-of-print catalog operators.
Libraries and nonprofit media archives compete indirectly by lending discs without commercial rental pricing.
current_dynamics: The industry is now defined by exit, not expansion. Redbox removed the last broad-based national kiosk network in 2024, Netflix removed the last scaled mail-subscription product in 2023, and Best Buy's 2024 retreat from DVD and Blu-ray retail reduced consumer visibility for discs. In 2025, DEG reported $62.2 billion of US home-entertainment spending, led by $57.5 billion in subscription streaming, while physical sell-through fell to $870 million. The remaining rental opportunity is mostly underserved broadband markets, older households, collectors, preservation-minded customers and titles unavailable on streaming.
whats_growing: Collector and preservation-oriented demand is the only meaningful pocket of growth. DEG reported 2025 4K UHD spending up 12% from 2024 even as total physical sell-through declined 9.3%. Specialty stores with rare, foreign, cult, local, out-of-print or director-focused catalogs can still attract enthusiasts. Digital substitutes are growing far faster: US subscription streaming reached $57.5 billion in 2025, and US video-game spending reached $60.8 billion in 2025, supported by subscriptions and digital content.
whats_shrinking: Mass-market DVD and Blu-ray rental, kiosk rental, subscription-by-mail rental, physical video-game rental and new-release walk-in rental are shrinking. DEG reported US physical home-entertainment sell-through down 23.4% in 2024 and another 9.3% in 2025, while BLS/FRED showed the NAICS 532282 employment index down 29.6% in 2025. Physical game demand is also moving digital, leaving rental operators with less inventory relevance and fewer high-velocity titles.
recent_developments: 2023-09-29: Netflix shipped its final DVD.com discs, ending its 25-year US DVD-by-mail rental service.
2024-01: Best Buy began ending DVD and Blu-ray sales in stores and online, reducing mainstream physical-media shelf space.
2024-07: Chicken Soup for the Soul Entertainment, Redbox's parent, moved into Chapter 7 liquidation and Redbox began shutting down roughly 24,000-27,000 kiosks.
2025-02-14: DEG reported 2024 US physical home-entertainment sell-through spending fell 23.4% to $959.59 million while subscription streaming topped $52 billion.
2026-02-11: DEG reported 2025 US physical home-entertainment sell-through fell another 9.3% to $870 million, while subscription streaming rose 19.8% to $57.5 billion.
2026-06-03: FRED/BLS data showed the 2025 NAICS 532282 employment index at 18.447, down 29.6% from 2024.
outlook: The outlook is continued contraction through 2026. The 2021 IBIS baseline forecast of $470.9 million in 2026 now looks optimistic because it predated the 2023 Netflix DVD shutdown and the 2024 Redbox liquidation. A 2026 market below $350 million is plausible if the 2025 employment-index proxy continues to track revenue, with surviving operators concentrated in niche catalogs, local loyalty, nonprofits and customers who value ownership, extras, offline access or unavailable titles. The industry will not recover as a mass-market rental channel without a major reversal in streaming economics or physical-media distribution.
one_sentence: The US DVD, game and video rental industry now consists mainly of small independent, kiosk-remnant, library-adjacent and collector-focused operators after Netflix DVD ended in 2023 and Redbox liquidated in 2024.
